title: Max Consecutive Ones III: sliding window allowing at most K zero flips.
shortTitle: Max Consecutive Ones III: Sliding Window Allowing At Most K Zero Flips
keyPoints: Variable-size sliding window that counts zeros inside the window
When the zero count exceeds K, shrink from the left until at most K zeros remain
The widest valid window seen is the answer: the longest achievable run of ones
No actual flipping is needed; counting zeros is enough because any window with at most K zeros can become all ones
K=0 reduces to the plain Max Consecutive Ones problem
O(n) time and O(1) space because both pointers only advance forward

s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a window counting zeros; keep it valid while zeros are at most K, and the widest such window is the answer.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Max Consecutive Ones III** – find the longest run of consecutive 1s obtainable in a binary array if you may flip at most K zeros to ones.
- **Variable sliding window** – grow the right edge counting zeros; shrink the left edge when the zero count exceeds K.
- **No actual flip** – any window with at most K zeros can be turned into all ones by flipping those zeros, so counting is sufficient.
- **K=0 case** – reduces to the plain Max Consecutive Ones problem with the count-and-reset approach.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time and O(1) space because both pointers only move forward.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India records daily service uptime as a binary string: 1 for up, 0 for down. The SLA rules allow excusing at most K down-days as planned maintenance. Rajesh finds the longest stretch of "up" days he can claim if he recolors at most K down-days as up, growing a window and shrinking it whenever it contains too many excused downs.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Max Consecutive Ones III asks for the longest run of ones achievable in a binary array if you may flip at most K zeros, and it is a clean variable-size sliding window. You grow the right edge counting zeros inside the window. As long as the zero count stays within the flip budget, the window is valid. When a new zero pushes the count above K, you shrink from the left until the count drops back to K.

The insight that makes this simple is that no actual flipping is needed. Any window containing at most K zeros can be turned into an unbroken run of ones by flipping exactly those zeros, so counting them is all you need. The window width directly equals the achievable run length.

This structure is more general than it looks. Setting K to zero gives the ordinary longest run of ones, and the same window solves the longest substring with at most K character replacements. The invariant is always the same: the window never holds more modifications than the budget allows.

In the service-level team at the National Bank of India, daily uptime is recorded as a binary string, and the SLA rules allow excusing up to K down-days as planned maintenance when computing the longest continuous availability stretch. The flip budget maps directly to excused outages, and the linear window handles long uptime histories efficiently.

Remember one sentence: count zeros in the window, shrink when the count exceeds K, and the widest valid window is the longest achievable run of ones.
